issues.failure_explanation: Assumption 1(iii) requires the KL inequality for every x in the open set Omega, which strictly contains X = dom p. For x in Omega \ X the stated conventions give partial Psi(x) = emptyset and dist(0, emptyset) = infinity, so L(x) = {y : F^*(x) - F(x,y) > 0} and (KL_y) becomes a global KL condition in y. The Example's inner problem x(cos y - 1) on [pi/4, pi] has a non-maximizing stationary point y = pi for every x > 0 (gradient -x sin(pi) = 0 lies in -N_{[pi/4,pi]}(pi) while the gap x(1+sqrt(2)/2) is positive), so the global KL fails for x just outside [1,2] as well as inside. Hence the Example does not satisfy Assumption 1(iii) as written, contradicting the Remark's claim, and the advertised 'local' assumption is in fact global on Omega \ X. This is not incidental: the proof of Theorem 1 uses the KL level set L(x) at points of U_epsilon \ X (needed for Rademacher/openness in Lemma lem:diff_ext), so the requirement outside X cannot simply be dropped.

failure_location.quote: For example, the minimax problem in Example~\eqref{example} satisfies the local KL condition but not the global one.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate Assumption 1(iii) so that for x in Omega \ X (or wherever partial Psi(x) is empty) the KL inequality is only required on a level set of fixed positive radius delta_bar, and restrict Theorem 1 and the algorithmic results to epsilon with gamma epsilon^sigma <= delta_bar; then re-verify the Example under the amended assumption.
issues.overall_effect: The paper's central claimed scope (a purely local KL condition, illustrated by the Example) is not what Assumption 1 states; the Remark's claim that the Example satisfies Assumption 1 is false under the stated conventions, and any problem for which the global KL fails at some x in Omega \ X is excluded.
issues.title: Local KL assumption degenerates to a global KL condition on Omega \ X, so the motivating Example does not satisfy Assumption 1 as stated
issues.why_classification: The results survive with a contained reformulation of the assumption and a parameter restriction, but the fix changes the hypotheses and the claimed scope rather than being a typo, and the motivating example claim must be re-established.

Then the total number of evaluations of the proximal operators of $p$ and $q$, and the gradient $\nabla f$ performed by Algorithm~\ref{algo_implement:whole} is at most $\widehat{K}_\epsilon$, $\widehat{N}_\epsilon$, and $\widehat{K}_\epsilon + \widehat{N}_\epsilon$, respectively

issues.failure_explanation: Step (step:constrained_PG) minimizes over the ball B(x^k, r), i.e. it is the proximal operator of p + I_{B(x^k,r)}, not of p. Assumption 1(ii) only provides exact prox of p. In general (e.g. p = ||.||_1 as in the numerical section, or p an indicator) the ball-constrained minimizer is not obtainable by a single prox-p evaluation; via Lagrangian duality it requires prox of p at a step size 1/(L_k + mu) with a multiplier mu found by a one-dimensional root search, i.e. possibly many prox-p evaluations and no exact finite procedure. Theorem 6's proof asserts one prox-p evaluation per iteration, which is therefore unsupported, and Algorithm 2 is not implementable with the oracle assumed in Assumption 1(ii).

failure_location.quote: x^{k+1} = \mathop{\arg\min}_{x \in \cB(x^k, r)} \Big\{ \langle \nabla_x f(x^{k}, y^{k}), x \rangle + \frac{L_k}{2} \|x - x^k\|^2 + p(x) \Big\}.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Strengthen the oracle assumption to exact computability of the ball-constrained proximal map x -> argmin_{x in B(x^k,r)} {<g,x> + (L/2)||x - x^k||^2 + p(x)} (or supply a finite/inexact inner procedure with its cost), and restate Theorem 6's prox-p count in terms of this oracle.
issues.overall_effect: The prox-p oracle count in Theorem 6 and the Remark's statement that O(K_hat) evaluations of the proximal operator of p suffice are unsupported; the implementability of Algorithm 2 under Assumption 1(ii) is not established. The gradient-evaluation and prox-q bounds are unaffected.
issues.title: Ball-constrained proximal step is not an evaluation of the assumed proximal operator of p; prox-p oracle count in Theorem 6 unsupported
issues.why_classification: The main rate guarantees survive, but the fix requires changing the assumed oracle (narrowing the class of 'simple' p for which the method is implementable as described) or adding an inner solver with its own complexity, which is more than a local typo-level repair.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: $ p: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\} $ is proper closed convex, $ q:\mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\} $ is proper closed convex
It then follows from $x^k \to x$ and the closedness of $\cX$ that $x\in\cX$.

issues.failure_explanation: A proper closed (lsc) convex function need not have a closed domain (e.g. q(y) = 1/y on (0, infinity), +infinity elsewhere). Lemma lem:QG's proof uses closedness of dom F(x,.) = dom q to conclude the limit y^* of Y(t_k) lies in dom F(x,.), and Lemma lem:open's proof uses closedness of X = dom p to conclude the limit x lies in X. Neither closedness follows from Assumption 1(ii), so as written both proofs rely on an unestablished premise. The conclusions are nevertheless true: in lem:QG upper semicontinuity of F(x,.) forces F(x,y^*) >= F^*(x) > -infinity, hence y^* in dom q; in lem:open the closedness of the graph of the convex subdifferential of p forces the limit of x^k (with bounded v^k in partial p(x^k)) to lie in dom p.

failure_location.quote: In addition, notice from Assumption \ref{ass:Lip_Smo_KL} that $\dom\,F(x, \cdot)$ is closed.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the closedness claims with the one-line arguments via upper semicontinuity of F(x,.) (lem:QG) and closedness of the graph of partial p (lem:open), or add 'dom p and dom q are closed' to Assumption 1(ii).
issues.overall_effect: As written, the proofs of Lemmas lem:QG and lem:open (and hence Theorem 1 and everything downstream) invoke a hypothesis absent from Assumption 1; the statements themselves remain correct after a local argument.
issues.title: Proofs assume closedness of dom q and dom p, which Assumption 1(ii) does not guarantee
issues.why_classification: A short, local, routine replacement argument (or a standard added hypothesis) preserves every statement and guarantee with no loss.
